A shambles is a situation, place, or thing that is in a state of complete disorder, confusion, or mess — so bad that it looks like everything has fallen apart or gone terribly wrong.

Think of it this way: if "messy" is a 3 out of 10, a shambles is a 9 or 10. It's not just untidy — it's chaotic, dysfunctional, and often beyond what you'd normally expect or accept.

Literally — to describe a physical place that is visibly wrecked or disordered:

"After the party, the house was a complete shambles — broken glasses everywhere, food on the floor, chairs knocked over."

Figuratively — to describe a situation, system, event, or organization that has gone badly wrong:

"The meeting was an absolute shambles. Nobody knew what to discuss, half the team was missing, and nothing was decided."
"The country's healthcare system is in shambles."

The figurative use is far more common in everyday speech today.

"Shambles" is a strong, critical word. When someone calls something a shambles, they're not mildly disappointed — they're saying it has failed badly or collapsed into chaos. There's often a sense of disbelief or frustration attached to it, like things that should have been organized simply weren't.

It can apply to almost anything: a plan, an event, a government, a relationship, a business, a room, a performance.

This is important: despite ending in -s, "shambles" is a singular noun. You say "it is a shambles", not "they are shambles."

You'll commonly see it in these forms:

  • "a shambles" → "The project is a shambles."
  • "in shambles" → "Their plans are in shambles."
  • "in a shambles" → "The office is in a shambles."

All three are correct and mean the same thing. "A shambles" and "in a shambles" are more common in British English, while "in shambles" (without the article "a") is more common in American English.
The words it loves to travel with

"Shambles" is almost always strengthened with an intensifier. People rarely say just "a shambles" — they tend to say:

  • a complete shambles
  • an absolute shambles
  • a total shambles
  • an utter shambles

This is because the word is already quite strong, and speakers use these intensifiers to make their frustration or disbelief even clearer.

"Shambles" is an informal word. You'll hear it in everyday conversation, in news commentary, in opinion pieces, and in casual writing. You wouldn't typically use it in a formal report or academic paper — there, you'd say something like "a state of complete disorganization" instead.

It is especially common in British English, where it's used very naturally in everyday speech and journalism. American English speakers use it too, but less frequently.
A few more examples to lock it in

"I studied all night, but the exam was a shambles — the questions made no sense."

"After the manager quit, the whole department fell into shambles."

"Don't ask me about my diet. It's been an utter shambles this month."

"The construction project is in shambles — they're three years behind schedule and way over budget."
If something is a shambles, it is in a state of serious chaos, mess, or disorder — far worse than just being a little disorganized, and usually implying that something has gone quite wrong.
